pathophysiology.summary: Chikungunya is an alphavirus infection spread mainly by day-biting Aedes mosquitoes, with cases in India peaking after the monsoon. The virus replicates in skin, muscle, joint and connective tissue, producing abrupt high fever, rash and severe, often symmetrical polyarthralgia. The acute phase lasts under 3 weeks; joint symptoms persist into a sub-acute phase (3 weeks to 3 months) and a chronic phase (beyond 3 months) in a proportion of patients, especially those over 45, women, and people with prior joint disease or severe early symptoms. Atypical disease affects the nervous system (meningoencephalitis, Guillain–Barré syndrome), heart, eye, kidney and liver, and is commoner in infants, adults over 65, pregnancy and people with diabetes, hypertension or cardiovascular disease. Vertical transmission occurs when maternal fever falls from 1 day before to 5 days after delivery, and neonates can develop severe disease. Treatment is symptomatic: there is no antiviral. Dengue is the key alternative diagnosis, so non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are withheld early until dengue is excluded.
keyMechanisms: Alphavirus replication in synovium, muscle and skin drives fever, rash and polyarthritis.
Persistent joint inflammation explains the sub-acute (3 weeks–3 months) and chronic (beyond 3 months) phases.
Neural, cardiac, renal and hepatic involvement produces atypical, potentially severe disease.
Peripartum maternal viraemia causes vertical transmission and neonatal disease.

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm the diagnosis and triage
actions: Ask about travel or residence and onset; record blood pressure, urine output and neurological state.
Send RT-PCR in the first week or IgM after day 7, plus a blood count to look for dengue.
Treat most patients at home with fluids, rest, cold packs to joints and tepid sponging.
Refer from primary care to a district or tertiary hospital and admit; triage by organ involvement.
Home care with paracetamol and review if worse.

clinicalManagement.title: Acute phase (under 3 weeks)
actions: Give paracetamol as first-line analgesic and antipyretic; add tramadol in adults if pain persists.
Do not give corticosteroids in the acute phase; avoid self-medication with antibiotics, steroids or other painkillers.
Do not give NSAIDs to children in the first 14 days; avoid NSAIDs in pregnancy.

clinicalManagement.title: Sub-acute phase (3 weeks to 3 months)
actions: Use an NSAID at full dose for mild pain (visual analogue scale 1–3); reassess in the first week and switch class by day 10 if inadequate.
Use oral prednisolone for severe polyarticular inflammation, moderate-to-severe pain or NSAID failure, for no more than 4 weeks in total.
Do not start disease-modifying drugs before 8 weeks.

clinicalManagement.title: Chronic phase (beyond 3 months)
actions: Hydroxychloroquine with an NSAID for 8–12 weeks.
Refer to rheumatology if inflammatory arthritis persists beyond 3 months; arrange physiotherapy.

clinicalManagement.title: Atypical, severe and neonatal disease
actions: Treat shock, heart failure, encephalitis and kidney injury as organ support in hospital; consider non-invasive ventilation for decompensated heart failure.
Neonates of mothers febrile around delivery: observe for days 3–7, test by RT-PCR, arrange echocardiography and long-term neurodevelopmental follow-up.

pathophysiology.summary: Acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) is a clinical label for fever of up to 5–7 days with altered mental status or new seizures. In India, Japanese encephalitis (JE), a flavivirus spread by Culex mosquitoes from pigs and wading birds, is an important cause, but treatable causes such as herpes simplex encephalitis, cerebral malaria, bacterial meningitis and scrub typhus must be covered while results are awaited. Brain inflammation causes cerebral oedema, raised intracranial pressure, seizures and coma; death follows herniation, status epilepticus, aspiration or shock. There is no antiviral for JE, so management is supportive: airway protection, circulatory support, control of seizures and intracranial pressure, normoglycaemia, fever control and nursing care, followed by rehabilitation for survivors with neurological deficits. Steroids are not indicated in viral encephalitis. Two doses of live attenuated JE vaccine are given in endemic districts under the Universal Immunization Programme.
keyMechanisms: Neurotropic viral infection (JE and others) inflames brain parenchyma, causing altered sensorium and seizures.
Cerebral oedema raises intracranial pressure and can lead to herniation.
Treatable mimics (herpes simplex, malaria, bacterial meningitis) need empirical therapy until excluded.
Survivors often carry neurological sequelae needing rehabilitation.

Obtain intravenous access, send samples and give 20 mL/kg normal saline for circulatory failure; add inotropes if needed.
Check glucose; treat fever with paracetamol and tepid sponging, not cold.

clinicalManagement.title: Stop seizures

Refractory seizures: transfer to a paediatric intensive care unit for midazolam infusion; without intensive care use valproate, levetiracetam or phenobarbitone.

Mannitol, or 3% saline when hypotensive, hypovolaemic or in renal failure (target sodium 145–155 mmol/L).
Short hyperventilation to arterial carbon dioxide 30–35 mmHg only for impending herniation.

Do not give steroids for viral encephalitis, including JE.
Treat the cause (for example antituberculous therapy with steroids for tuberculous meningitis) and stop unneeded empirical drugs.

pathophysiology.summary: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) is caused by Leishmania donovani, transmitted by sandflies, and in India is concentrated in Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh. The parasite multiplies inside macrophages of the spleen, liver and bone marrow, causing prolonged fever, massive splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, weight loss and pancytopenia. Untreated disease is usually fatal through secondary infection, bleeding or wasting. A recombinant-antigen rapid diagnostic test (rK39-type) detects antibody with sensitivity and specificity above 90% and is the programme's diagnostic standard; it stays positive for months to years and cannot diagnose relapse. The national first-line treatment is a single dose of liposomal amphotericin B 10 mg/kg. Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) is a skin form appearing after apparent cure (85–90%) or without prior illness (5–6%), with hypopigmented macules, papules or nodules, often on the face, with preserved sensation; people with PKDL act as a parasite reservoir, so treating them supports elimination.
keyMechanisms: Intracellular parasites in macrophages enlarge the spleen and liver and suppress the marrow (pancytopenia).
Immune dysfunction and cytopenias predispose to secondary infection and bleeding.
Persistent dermal parasites after treatment cause PKDL, which keeps transmission going.
Liposomal amphotericin B delivers drug to infected macrophages with lower nephrotoxicity than conventional amphotericin.

pathophysiology.summary: Lymphatic filariasis in India is caused mainly by Wuchereria bancrofti (and Brugia malayi in parts of the south and east), transmitted by Culex and other mosquitoes. Adult worms live in lymphatic vessels and release microfilariae into the blood. Worm-induced lymphatic dilatation and inflammation, worsened by repeated bacterial skin infections, cause acute adenolymphangitis attacks with fever and painful swelling, and over years produce irreversible lymphoedema, elephantiasis and hydrocele. Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia is an allergic lung response to microfilariae with nocturnal cough, wheeze and very high eosinophil counts. India's elimination programme gives annual mass drug administration of diethylcarbamazine (DEC) with albendazole to everyone eligible in endemic districts; this interrupts transmission but does not reverse established lymphoedema or hydrocele, which need hygiene-based morbidity care and surgery.

Recurrent bacterial skin infections of damaged limbs drive acute attacks and progression to elephantiasis.
Microfilariae in the lung trigger tropical pulmonary eosinophilia.
Annual DEC plus albendazole reduces microfilariae and transmission.

pathophysiology.summary: Leptospirosis is a bacterial zoonosis caused by pathogenic Leptospira shed in the urine of rats, cattle and other animals. In India it peaks in the monsoon in coastal states such as Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Karnataka and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, often among farmers and people wading through flood water. Spirochaetes enter through cut skin or mucosa, disseminate in the blood and damage small vessels. Most infections are anicteric and self-limiting, with fever, severe calf and lumbar myalgia and conjunctival suffusion; 5–10% develop severe disease (Weil's disease) with jaundice, acute kidney injury, pulmonary haemorrhage, myocarditis and shock. Pulmonary haemorrhage is the commonest cause of death. Transaminases are only mildly raised while creatine kinase is markedly high, which helps separate leptospirosis from viral hepatitis. Early antibiotics (doxycycline for mild disease, intravenous penicillin or a third-generation cephalosporin for severe disease) and organ support are the core of treatment.
keyMechanisms: Spirochaetes enter through abraded skin or mucosa and spread in the blood.
Vasculitis and endothelial injury cause haemorrhage, conjunctival suffusion and pulmonary bleeding.
Tubular necrosis and interstitial nephritis cause acute kidney injury, often non-oliguric with hypokalaemia.
Hepatocellular dysfunction produces jaundice with only mildly raised transaminases; muscle injury raises creatine kinase.

pathophysiology.summary: Nipah virus is a henipavirus whose natural reservoir is fruit bats (Pteropus). In India, outbreaks have occurred in West Bengal and repeatedly in Kerala. People are infected through food contaminated by bats, such as raw date palm sap or bat-bitten fruit, and through close contact with infected people's body fluids, which makes hospital transmission a recognised risk. After an incubation of 6–21 days (under 2 weeks in 90%), the virus causes a vasculitis with endothelial and neuronal infection. Illness begins with fever, headache, vomiting and myalgia and progresses to encephalitis with drowsiness, segmental myoclonus, autonomic signs and coma, sometimes with cough or breathlessness. Case fatality in confirmed cases is 40–75%; 20–30% of survivors keep neurological deficits, and relapse or late-onset encephalitis can occur up to 4 years later. There is no proven antiviral, so care is supportive, delivered in strict isolation, with rapid notification and 21-day follow-up of contacts.

Systemic vasculitis and neuronal infection cause encephalitis with myoclonus and autonomic instability.

pathophysiology.summary: Melioidosis is infection with Burkholderia pseudomallei, a soil and water bacterium of tropical regions. In India most reported cases come from coastal Karnataka (Udupi has the highest reported incidence) and Tamil Nadu, and cases rise with monsoon rainfall. Infection follows skin inoculation, inhalation or aspiration, especially in farmers. Diabetes is the main risk factor, with alcohol misuse, chronic kidney or lung disease, thalassaemia and steroid use also important. The organism survives inside cells and forms abscesses; illness ranges from fulminant bacteraemic pneumonia and septic shock to localised abscesses of the liver, spleen, prostate, parotid, muscle or bone. Culture is the diagnostic standard, so the laboratory must be told to look for it. Treatment has an intravenous intensive phase (ceftazidime or meropenem for at least 2 weeks) followed by an oral eradication phase with co-trimoxazole for 3–6 months to prevent relapse. Mortality ranges from 9% to 70% depending on access to care.
keyMechanisms: Inoculation, inhalation or aspiration of soil organisms, favoured by diabetes and other immune defects.
Intracellular survival leads to bacteraemia and abscesses in liver, spleen, prostate and other organs.
Intracellular persistence causes relapse unless a prolonged eradication phase is completed.
The organism is intrinsically resistant to many antibiotics, so empirical regimens for sepsis can miss it.

pathophysiology.summary: Kyasanur Forest disease is a tick-borne flavivirus haemorrhagic fever first reported in Shimoga district, Karnataka, in 1957, and now found across the Western Ghats in Karnataka, Kerala, Goa, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu. Haemaphysalis ticks, especially nymphs, transmit the virus; deaths of langurs and bonnet monkeys often signal activity, because dying monkeys drop infected ticks. The season runs from October–November, peaks January to April and falls by May–June. After 3–8 days' incubation, a first phase of sudden high fever, headache, myalgia and prostration lasts 5–12 days, with leucopenia (the most sensitive laboratory marker), thrombocytopenia, raised transaminases, raised haematocrit from capillary leak, and bleeding. Some patients have a second phase from about day 8 with headache and meningoencephalitis. There is no specific antiviral; care is supportive with fluids guided by haematocrit and management of bleeding and neurological complications.

Central nervous system involvement causes a second-phase meningoencephalitis.

pathophysiology.summary: Brucellosis is a zoonosis caused by Brucella species (B. melitensis, B. abortus, B. suis), acquired in India mainly from raw milk and milk products and from close contact with cattle, goats, sheep and pigs, including handling births and abortions in animals; laboratory exposure is also recognised. After an incubation of 5 days to 6 months (average 2–4 weeks), intracellular infection of the reticuloendothelial system causes fever (often undulant), sweats, malaise, arthralgia, back pain, weight loss and hepatosplenomegaly. Focal disease affects bones and joints, the genitourinary tract, the heart (endocarditis, the main cause of death) and the nervous system. Symptoms are non-specific, so diagnosis needs culture or serology, and the laboratory must be warned because the organism is a hazard to staff. Treatment needs combination antibiotics for at least 6 weeks; doxycycline with an aminoglycoside relapses less than doxycycline with rifampicin.

Intracellular persistence explains relapse after short or single-drug treatment.

title: Rickettsial infections other than scrub typhus (India)

evidenceAudit.scope: Spotted fever group rickettsioses (including Indian tick typhus) and murine typhus in India: suspicion, testing and doxycycline-first treatment; scrub typhus has its own topic.
findings: Clinical features, laboratory findings, case definitions, tests and adult, paediatric, pregnancy and severe-disease doses checked against DHR-ICMR 2015 (pp. 2, 12–18).
Organism coverage (R. conorii, R. typhi) and 7-day course cross-checked against ICMR 2019 (Table 2.1 row 4, p. 10; Table 2.2, p. 11).
Not clinically reviewed.
unverifiedSections: DHR-ICMR 2015 focuses on scrub typhus; its case definitions and test cut-offs are applied here to rickettsial infection generally.
No paediatric chloramphenicol dose is given separately.
Defervescence timing after doxycycline is not stated in the sources.
CKD and CLD adjustment lines are general cautions.
Normal values are typical adult ranges unless labelled otherwise; local laboratory ranges apply.

pathophysiology.summary: Rickettsiae are small intracellular bacteria that infect vascular endothelium. Besides scrub typhus, India has spotted fever group rickettsioses, notably Indian tick typhus (Rickettsia conorii) transmitted by ticks, and murine typhus (R. typhi) transmitted by rat fleas. Endothelial infection causes a small-vessel vasculitis, which explains the rash, which typically appears 3–5 days after onset as pink blanching macules that may become maculopapular, petechial or haemorrhagic, as well as oedema, thrombocytopenia and organ involvement. Complications, usually after the first week, include jaundice, kidney failure, pneumonitis, acute respiratory distress, myocarditis, meningoencephalitis and shock. No single sign is diagnostic, so geography, occupation and exposure guide suspicion. Doxycycline is the drug of choice and should be started on suspicion, without waiting for test results; azithromycin is used in pregnancy and as an alternative.
keyMechanisms: Tick or flea bite introduces rickettsiae that infect endothelial cells.
Small-vessel vasculitis produces rash, oedema and haemorrhage.
Endothelial damage and consumption cause thrombocytopenia and multi-organ dysfunction.
Intracellular location explains response to doxycycline, azithromycin or chloramphenicol but not beta-lactams.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Eschar typical; same doxycycline treatment.
Leucopenia, rising haematocrit and plasma leakage.
Rapidly progressive purpura with shock; Gram-negative diplococci.
Prodromal cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots.
Water exposure, calf tenderness, jaundice and kidney injury.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Acute undifferentiated fever of 5 days or more, with or without eschar (DHR-ICMR 2015, p. 14).
Suspected case with Weil–Felix titre 1:80 or more and IgM ELISA optical density above 0.5 (p. 14).
Rickettsial DNA on PCR of blood or eschar, or rising titre in paired sera by immunofluorescence (p. 14).
